program_overview.title: Waterloo Math Contests: Gauss to Euclid
program_overview.tagline: One problem-solving toolkit, three grade tracks: from the first Gauss counting ideas to the clear, complete written solutions the Euclid asks for.
program_overview.description:
The Centre for Education in Mathematics and Computing (CEMC) at the University of Waterloo runs a family of math contests "Designed by teams of expert mathematicians and educators for Grades 5 to 12". Each contest is matched to a grade. The Gauss Contest is for "Students in Grades 7 and 8.", and CEMC adds that "Motivated students in lower grades are welcome to write the contest." The Pascal, Cayley and Fermat Contests are for Grade 9, Grade 10 and Grade 11. The Fryer, Galois and Hypatia Contests are for the same three grades, with "4 questions; a mix of final answer-only and full-solution." The Euclid Contest is for "Students in their final year of secondary school or CÉGEP students." and has "10 questions; a mix of final answer only and full-solution." The CIMC is for Grades 9 and 10 and the CSMC for Grades 11 and 12 and CÉGEP students, each with "9 questions; 6 are answer only and 3 are full-solution."

For the 2026/27 contest year CEMC lists the CIMC and CSMC on Wednesday, November 18, 2026; the Pascal, Cayley and Fermat Contests on Tuesday, February 23, 2027 and Wednesday, February 24, 2027; the Euclid on Tuesday, April 6, 2027; the Fryer, Galois and Hypatia on Wednesday, April 7, 2027; and the Gauss from Monday, May 10, 2027 to Friday, May 21, 2027 (dates for North and South America). Students write through their school: CEMC says "It is not possible for students to individually register for a contest" and "all students must participate through their school."

This course teaches the mathematics behind all of these contests in three grade tracks, and it teaches the two skills they test in different ways: fast, accurate work on multiple-choice and answer-only questions, and full solutions that explain every step. Practice comes from two places: our own original problems written for each topic, and CEMC's free past contests, which CEMC publishes with no registration or fee and which students work where CEMC publishes them. We never copy CEMC problems into our materials. We teach the ideas and the habits, and we make no promise of scores, certificates of distinction, prizes, scholarships or admissions.
what_makes_this_different: Built around CEMC's contests by grade: Gauss for Grades 7 and 8, then Pascal, Cayley, Fermat, Fryer, Galois, Hypatia, CIMC, CSMC and Euclid
Three grade tracks taught in separate batches, so every student works on problems at the right level
Full-solution writing taught directly: stating the idea, showing every step and checking the answer, as the full-solution contests require
Our own original problems for every topic, plus CEMC's free past contests used as practice where CEMC publishes them
A timed practice round every month, in the format of the contest each student will write next
Honest about entry and results: students write through their school, and we promise learning, not scores

faqs.question: What are the Waterloo math contests?
faqs.answer: They are the math contests run by CEMC (the Centre for Education in Mathematics and Computing) at the University of Waterloo, "Designed by teams of expert mathematicians and educators for Grades 5 to 12". This course covers the Gauss, Pascal, Cayley, Fermat and Euclid Contests, the Fryer, Galois and Hypatia Contests, and the CIMC and CSMC. CEMC also says: "Our contests are not tests or exams. There is no passing or failing score."

faqs.question: Which contest should my child write?
faqs.answer: CEMC matches each contest to a grade. Gauss is for "Students in Grades 7 and 8." Pascal is for Grade 9, Cayley for Grade 10 and Fermat for Grade 11. Fryer, Galois and Hypatia are for Grades 9, 10 and 11. The CIMC is for Grades 9 and 10, the CSMC for Grades 11 and 12 and CÉGEP students, and the Euclid for "Students in their final year of secondary school or CÉGEP students." In the first two weeks we place each student on a track and plan the contests for the year.

faqs.question: When are the 2026/27 contests?
faqs.answer: CEMC lists these dates for North and South America: CIMC and CSMC on Wednesday, November 18, 2026; Pascal, Cayley and Fermat on Tuesday, February 23, 2027 and Wednesday, February 24, 2027; Euclid on Tuesday, April 6, 2027; Fryer, Galois and Hypatia on Wednesday, April 7, 2027; and Gauss from Monday, May 10, 2027 to Friday, May 21, 2027. Schools order the contests before CEMC's deadlines, so check the current dates on CEMC's site with your school.

faqs.question: How do we register for a contest?
faqs.answer: Through a school, not through us. CEMC says "It is not possible for students to individually register for a contest" and "all students must participate through their school." If a student's school does not take part, CEMC suggests that "students can look for another local school that will allow them to join as a participant". We remind families to check the school's order early.

faqs.question: What is the difference between multiple-choice and full-solution contests?
faqs.answer: Gauss, Pascal, Cayley and Fermat each have 25 multiple-choice questions in 60 minutes, so speed and accuracy matter most. Fryer, Galois and Hypatia have "4 questions; a mix of final answer-only and full-solution." in 75 minutes, and the Euclid has "10 questions; a mix of final answer only and full-solution." in 2.5 hours. On a full-solution question the reasoning is marked, not just the answer, so we teach students to write clear, complete solutions.

faqs.question: Do you use CEMC past contests?
faqs.answer: Yes, the way CEMC intends. CEMC says "There is no registration or fee required to access these materials." and its past contests page says "Below you will find resources from the last 10 years." We set those past contests as practice, which students work on CEMC's site, and review them in class beside our own original problems. We never copy CEMC problems into our materials.

faqs.question: Will this course get my child a certificate of distinction or a top score?
faqs.answer: No course can promise that, and we do not. Results depend on the student, the paper and the day. What the course gives is steady practice, timed rounds, written feedback on full solutions and an error log, so progress is visible month by month.

faqs.question: Do the Waterloo contests matter for university?
faqs.answer: They are a good challenge, not a requirement. The University of Waterloo's Computer Science page says writing the CSMC or Euclid "is not required for admission, but writing one of these contests is required for some scholarships offered by the Faculty of Mathematics." Waterloo's Admission Information Form also says "This form asks about any Waterloo mathematics contests you've participated in". Always check each university's current pages. We make no admission or scholarship promises.

faqs.question: Can a younger student write the Gauss?
faqs.answer: CEMC says "Motivated students in lower grades are welcome to write the contest." This course starts at about age 11. A younger student who is strong in math can join the Gauss track after the free demo class, if the teacher agrees the level fits.

faqs.question: Does my child need to be top of the class in math?
faqs.answer: No. A student should be comfortable with school math for their grade and willing to work on problems that take time. Contest problems feel unfamiliar at first for almost everyone; the course builds the habits that make them approachable, one idea at a time.

faqs.question: How are the classes run?
faqs.answer: Live online classes, twice a week, with a real teacher, in a group of 15 to 20 students, a mini batch of up to 6, or 1-on-1. Each grade track is taught in its own batches. Weekdays or weekends, flexible: choose your batch, or for a very personalised plan choose 1-on-1 at your convenience, weekend mornings or weekdays. Current fees for your region are shown in the pricing section of this page.

faqs.question: Can we try a class first?
faqs.answer: Yes. Book a free demo class. The teacher works through a short original problem with your child, suggests the right track and contests for the year, and recommends group, mini batch or 1-on-1 classes. There is no obligation to enrol.
